title: Can Mexico thread the needle between Washington and Beijing?
gist: Mexico faces its own 'China Shock 2.0' — a ~$120 billion annual trade deficit with China and fiscal pressure that makes tariffs attractive — so it is likely to accommodate US demands for restrictions on competing Chinese goods in USMCA talks. But because over half its Chinese imports are intermediate inputs, the authors expect Mexico to resist curbs on critical inputs, push back on Peter Navarro's expansive 'transshipment' definition, screen investment in critical infrastructure while keeping manufacturing FDI largely open.

insights.claim: Mexico faces the same 'China Shock 2.0' as the rest of the world, driven by Chinese policies that constrain domestic consumption and provide state support to exporters, so its tariffs on China are not simply a response to US pressure.
insights.so_what: Mexican tariffs on China are domestically anchored and likely sticky regardless of US talks.

insights.claim: China's 2025 current account surplus was 3.8 percent of GDP, the highest in sixteen years; though below the 9.8 percent 2007 peak, the $735 billion raw figure is 75 percent higher than in 2007, and China is now 20 percent of global GDP, twice its 2007 share.
insights.so_what: China's surplus is larger in absolute terms than ever, and diverted from the US, pressures third markets.

insights.claim: At the G20 meeting in Asheville, all participating countries except China called for countries with excessive and persistent external surpluses to remove distortions that constrain domestic consumption.
insights.so_what: Growing global consensus against Chinese surplus policies supports more trade defense worldwide.

insights.claim: Mexico's trade deficit with China has doubled in the past decade to roughly $120 billion a year, with shoemakers in León, auto parts and household appliance makers complaining of overwhelming Chinese competition and lobbying the government.
insights.so_what: Domestic industrial lobbying sustains protectionist pressure in Mexico.

insights.claim: Mexico's rising debt ratios and at-risk investment-grade rating make tariffs an attractive revenue source that is hard to unwind; the tariffs worked, with imports from China and others falling sharply in H1 2026.
insights.so_what: Sovereign credit pressure is a hidden driver of Mexican trade policy; tariff revenue is now fiscally embedded.
insights.quote: That makes tariffs an especially attractive source of revenue and difficult to unwind.

insights.speaker: Atlantic Council

insights.claim: The US undermines its case against China by making similar allegations against sixty other countries via Section 301 excess capacity investigations, met with disbelief by Mexican business leaders.
insights.so_what: Indiscriminate US trade actions reduce allied buy-in for a focused anti-China coalition.
insights.quote: “wouldn’t that be nice?” is a typical rejoinder from Mexican business leaders
insights.locator: Notwithstanding its efforts at the G20
insights.speaker: Atlantic Council

insights.claim: Some form of Mexican tariffs on Chinese goods is likely to remain in place regardless of trade-talk outcomes, and Mexico may prove receptive to US pressure to prolong or add tariffs, partly because it exports little to China, limiting retaliation risk.
insights.so_what: Base case: persistent Mexican tariff wall on Chinese goods, supportive of USMCA-aligned supply chains.
insights.locator: But that does not mean Washington
insights.speaker: Atlantic Council

insights.claim: Just over half of Mexico's imports from China are intermediate goods — a higher share than in Canada or the US — and domestic manufacturers relying on them have pushed back, limiting the level and scope of tariffs, especially in auto parts.
insights.so_what: Mexican export manufacturing remains dependent on Chinese inputs; expect exemptions for critical inputs.
insights.locator: But there are limits to Mexico’s willingness
insights.speaker: Atlantic Council

insights.claim: Mexico is likely to be more receptive to broad US pressure than Latin American peers because of its US dependence, but more resistant to restrictions on intermediate goods because it is the region's only manufacturing export powerhouse; it will likely keep exempting critical products or applying lower rates.
insights.so_what: Rules-of-origin negotiations are the medium-term risk to inputs currently spared tariffs.
insights.speaker: Atlantic Council

insights.claim: White House advisor Peter Navarro's expansive view of 'transshipment' appears to treat any use of foreign inputs — and even Chinese ownership or financing — as transshipment, which could implicate virtually any manufacturing exporter to the US, including Mexico; whether he speaks for the administration is unclear.
insights.so_what: A broad transshipment standard is a tail risk for Mexican manufacturing exports and nearshoring investment.
insights.locator: While a certain degree of resistance
insights.speaker: Atlantic Council

insights.claim: Under Navarro's logic, cars from a General Motors plant in Querétaro would be considered US rather than Mexican exports, illustrating how ownership-based tests could scramble trade classification.
insights.so_what: Ownership-based origin rules would create legal uncertainty for multinational plants in Mexico.
insights.locator: That’s true not just of trade
insights.speaker: Atlantic Council

insights.claim: On August 30 Mexico's Congress moved closer to passing a CFIUS-like national security screening mechanism for foreign acquisitions, following a December 2023 agreement between Janet Yellen and Rogelio Ramírez de la O.
insights.so_what: Passage would boost US negotiators' confidence in USMCA talks and restrict Chinese investment in ports and border infrastructure.

insights.claim: Mexico currently lacks a mechanism to block problematic investments, many initiated by state or local governments with limited visibility from Mexico City.
insights.so_what: Subnational investment deals are a blind spot in North American security screening.

insights.claim: For most manufacturing investment Mexico should keep a permissive regime, since building North American supply chains requires foreign suppliers; Chinese FDI is no more than 10 percent of total FDI even accounting for underreporting, though its greenfield share has likely grown.
insights.so_what: Chinese capital is a modest share of Mexican FDI; broad bans would cost more than they protect.
insights.speaker: Atlantic Council

insights.claim: Mexican tariffs on countries without trade agreements could unintentionally hit major FDI sources South Korea and Taiwan, and the lack of a federal investment promotion office favors wealthy states like Querétaro, Nuevo León and Chihuahua.
insights.so_what: Second-order risk to Korean and Taiwanese nearshoring investment in Mexico.
insights.locator: Moreover, Mexico’s tariffs may have consequences
insights.speaker: Atlantic Council

insights.claim: Where US bans products from Chinese parent companies in sensitive sectors, Mexican plants become commercially unviable because the domestic market is too small — as BYD apparently concluded in 2025 when it halted plans for a Mexican factory.
insights.so_what: Chinese EV and sensitive-tech makers are effectively locked out of using Mexico as a US-market platform.
